title: Build a Self-Organizing Agent Swarm: No Central Scheduler
description: Agents announce roles on a pub/sub topic, form trust in pairs, and send work straight to the fastest peer with the right role. A Python tutorial on Pilot.
seoTitle: Build a Self-Organizing Agent Swarm: No Central Scheduler
author: Pilot Protocol editorial team

children.text: This tutorial shows you how to build an agent swarm that organizes its own work. Most multi-agent systems have one central process that decides who does what, and that process becomes the bottleneck: when it goes down, gets overloaded, or has to be trusted with everything, the whole system suffers. Here, every agent runs the same code and makes its own decisions:
agents announce their role, build their own view of who else is around, set up trust with each other in pairs, and send work straight to a peer with the right role
. One Pilot daemon acts as a meeting point for announcements, but it never assigns work.

By the end, you will have a Python script that you run once per machine. Each copy joins the swarm, finds peers through announcements on a pub/sub topic, exchanges work with them through Pilot's encrypted tunnels, and favours the peers that answer fastest.
, one per machine or container, each with its own Pilot daemon and a role (summarizer, analyzer, reviewer, translator)
: one Pilot daemon whose built-in pub/sub broker carries a roster topic. It relays announcements and does nothing else.
that each agent builds for itself from those announcements, with entries that expire when an agent goes quiet
: every agent asks every peer for a trust handshake; when both sides have asked, the daemons approve it on their own
for task execution (each agent calls an LLM to process work)
: each agent picks among peers with the right role, weighted toward the ones that answered fastest, and retries elsewhere when one does not answer
The architecture relies on three Pilot Protocol features:
Why a roster and not a search?
Pilot has no network-wide search for your own nodes.
attaches up to three labels to a node, but nothing queries the network by tag.

is the directory of the public data service agents, not of your machines. A private node's hostname resolves only for itself, for peers that trust it, and for members of a network it belongs to. So agents have to tell each other who they are, and a pub/sub topic is the simplest place to do that.
The public backbone (the default registry) or a registry you run yourself
An OpenAI API key (or any LLM API) for task execution

import json
import os
import random
import subprocess
import sys
import threading
import time

HUB = os.environ["SWARM_HUB"]   # the hub daemon's address, e.g. 0:0000.0000.1A2B
ROSTER = "swarm.roster"          # exact topic name on the hub's broker
ANNOUNCE_EVERY = 30              # seconds between announcements
ROSTER_TTL = 90                  # forget peers not heard from for this long
ASK_AGAIN = 300                  # re-send an unanswered handshake after this long
TASK_FOR_ROLE = {
    "summarizer": "summarize",
    "analyzer": "analyze",
    "reviewer": "code_review",
    "translator": "translate",
}

def pilotctl(*args, timeout=30):
    """Run pilotctl --json and return the "data" part of its reply."""
    out = subprocess.run(["pilotctl", "--json", *args],
                         capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=timeout)
    if out.returncode != 0:
        raise RuntimeError(out.stderr.strip() or out.stdout.strip())
    return json.loads(out.stdout)["data"]

def node_id(address):
    """'0:0000.0000.1A2B' -> 0x1A2B (the last two groups are the node ID)."""
    return int(address.split(":", 1)[1].split(".", 1)[1].replace(".", ""), 16)

def trusted_ids():
    return {int(t["node_id"]) for t in pilotctl("trust")["trusted"]}

class SwarmAgent:
    def __init__(self, role):
        self.role = role
        me = pilotctl("info")
        self.address = me["address"]
        self.node_id = int(me["node_id"])
        self.hostname = f"swarm-{role}-{self.node_id}"
        self.peers = {}        # address -> role, hostname, node_id, seen, latency, asked
        self.lock = threading.Lock()
        self.handled = set()   # message IDs of requests already answered

children.text: returns this daemon's address and node ID. The hostname is only a readable label; it includes the node ID because hostnames are unique on a registry.

The hub is an ordinary Pilot daemon. Every daemon runs a small pub/sub broker on port 1002, so any machine all your agents can reach will do; a small VM is fine. Keep it private (the default): a private daemon only accepts tunnels from peers it trusts, so only agents you approved can read or write the roster.

# On the hub
pilotctl daemon start
pilotctl --json info        # note "address": the agents get it as SWARM_HUB

# As agents ask to join
pilotctl pending             # node IDs and their justification
pilotctl approve <node_id>

children.text: Approving by hand is the safe default. For a demo on machines you control, a short loop on the hub can approve requests that carry the swarm's join text:

fields.code:
# hub_approver.py: on the hub, approve handshakes from swarm workers
import json
import subprocess
import time

JOIN = "swarm worker, role "

while True:
    out = subprocess.run(["pilotctl", "--json", "pending"], capture_output=True, text=True)
    for req in json.loads(out.stdout)["data"]["pending"]:
        if req.get("justification", "").startswith(JOIN):
            subprocess.run(["pilotctl", "approve", str(int(req["node_id"]))])
    time.sleep(5)

children.text: Anyone who knows the hub's address and the phrase gets in with this loop. Outside a demo, approve by hand or keep an allowlist of node IDs.

A handshake is a request, not a connection: it waits on the hub until the hub approves it. Once approved, both daemons hold a trust record bound to each other's Ed25519 key, and the agent can open tunnels to the hub.
Every agent publishes a small announcement to
on the hub every 30 seconds and keeps a subscription to the same topic open. Topics match exactly, so the name just has to be the same everywhere.

The roster tells an agent who exists. It does not let them talk: by default, agents are
, and a private daemon refuses tunnels from peers it does not trust. Each pair of agents needs its own trust record.

This is where the swarm sets itself up without an operator. When agent X asks Y for trust, the request waits on Y. When Y asks X in turn, X's daemon sees that it has an open request to Y, treats the pair as mutual, approves on its own and tells Y, and both sides are trusted. Because every agent asks every peer it sees, each pair ends up mutual within one or two rounds, and nobody approves anything by hand after the hub.
The flip side is that trust follows the roster: any agent the hub approved can join every pair. That is why the hub's approval is the real admission control for the swarm.

Each agent keeps a running average of how long each peer took to answer and picks among trusted peers with the right role, weighted toward the fastest. A peer that has not answered yet counts as one second. A failure is recorded as a 120-second answer, so a failing peer is still tried now and then and can earn its way back.

fields.code:
def pick_peer(self, role, exclude=()):
        """Choose a trusted peer with the role, favouring fast responders."""
        trusted = trusted_ids()
        cands = [(a, p) for a, p in self.live_peers()
                 if p["role"] == role and p["node_id"] in trusted and a not in exclude]
        if not cands:
            return None
        weights = [1.0 / (p["latency"] or 1.0) for _, p in cands]
        return random.choices([a for a, _ in cands], weights=weights)[0]

    def record_latency(self, addr, seconds):
        with self.lock:
            old = self.peers[addr]["latency"]
            self.peers[addr]["latency"] = seconds if old is None else 0.7 * old + 0.3 * seconds

What Organizes Itself, and What Does Not
Run the swarm for a while and this is what the code does on its own:
New agents appear in every roster within one announcement interval of being approved by the hub. Agents that stop announcing disappear after 90 seconds.
Each pair of agents becomes mutually trusted once both have asked, with no operator involved.
Work for a role spreads across the agents that have it, and shifts toward the ones that answer fastest. An agent that stops answering gets less work until it recovers.

What it does not do: there is no queue, so a request that fails three times is dropped and the caller decides what to do. There is no global view of load; each agent only knows the latencies it has measured itself. And the hub is a shared dependency for membership. If it goes down, agents keep their trust records and keep working with the peers in their rosters until those entries expire; new agents cannot join until it is back. Raise
to ride out longer hub outages, or run two hubs and subscribe to both.
the only central piece is a relay for announcements. Who works with whom, who trusts whom, and who gets the next task are decided by the agents themselves.

If You Run Your Own Registry

On a registry you operate, a private network can replace the hub. Creating a network needs that registry's admin token, which is why this only works on your own registry; on the public backbone only its operators can create networks. Start every daemon with

fields.code:
# Once, with the registry's admin token
PILOT_ADMIN_TOKEN=... pilotctl network create --name swarm --join-rule token --token <join-secret>

# On each agent
pilotctl network join <network_id> --token <join-secret>
pilotctl --json network members <network_id>

children.text: Three things change. The member list is the roster: it returns every member's node ID and hostname, so put the role in the hostname (as the script already does) and read it from there. Hostnames of members resolve for each other. And a handshake between two members of the same network is approved automatically, so the pairwise trust step still runs but never waits. See the
A few things grow with the size of the swarm:
Full mesh trust is n(n-1)/2 pairs: 45 for 10 agents, 4,950 for 100. For a large swarm, only ask for trust from peers in roles you exchange work with.
Every announcement goes to every subscriber, so the hub's fan-out grows with the square of the swarm size. Announce less often as the swarm grows.
A topic can have up to 1,000 subscribers, and each publishing connection may send 100 events per second (bursts of 200). One announcement every 30 seconds per agent is far below that.
Narrowing trust to the roles you use is a small change in
Both sides of a pair must ask for the request to become mutual, so pick the roles symmetrically: if summarizers send work to analyzers, analyzers should also ask summarizers.

The patterns here (a shared announcement topic, pairwise trust, direct requests with replies, and routing that learns from latency) are building blocks for larger multi-agent systems. What is missing is just as important: no scheduler, no work queue, no service mesh and no load balancer. For a simpler introduction to the same concepts, see
